title: PMU-Faker: The Apparently Harmless Performance Monitoring Unit Events Are Actually Harmful
evidence_span: A fuzzing framework identifies 118 vulnerable PMU events; PMU-Faker uses two timing mechanisms with different granularity to implement timing side channels without a conventional timer, with demonstrations against transient execution, AES key extraction, Intel SGX, and cross-VM information leakage.
problem: Performance monitoring events that appear securely implemented can still expose timing signals usable to construct side-channel attacks without an explicit timer.
method_or_artifact: Automated PMU-event fuzzing and PMU-Faker timing mechanisms balancing precision and adaptability across instruction-triggered cycle variation.
workload_or_benchmark: 118 discovered PMU events and four attack demonstrations; processor generations, OS/hypervisor, event configurations, leakage rates, and mitigations are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Modern CPU performance-monitoring units, transient execution, AES, SGX, and virtualized environments; microarchitecture, privilege model, and PMU access controls are unspecified.
limits: The description omits platform coverage, exploit prerequisites, timing resolution, leakage rates, false positives, and mitigation cost.
Attack demonstrations establish feasibility but not prevalence across processors or cloud deployments.
Official description only; security claims require paper-level and responsible-disclosure verification.

title: Beyond Exact: Tight WCET Analysis of GPU Kernels with Branch Divergence
evidence_span: The work models timing anomalies from branch divergence, derives exact GPU-thread-block WCET under prior scheduling constraints without fixed warp-path assumptions, and adds a practical warp-execution constraint; experiments report 19.13% average and up to 39.39% reduction in WCET estimates.
problem: Branch divergence and black-box warp scheduling make GPU worst-case execution-time bounds either unrealistic or overly pessimistic for real-time systems.
method_or_artifact: Static exact WCET analysis for divergent GPU thread blocks plus a practical warp-execution constraint yielding tighter bounds.
workload_or_benchmark: GPU kernels and thread-block timing analyses with divergent control flow; GPU architecture, kernel suite, scheduler model, and comparison bounds are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: GPU warps, thread blocks, and a scheduler treated as a black box under relaxed assumptions; vendor architecture, frequency, memory behavior, and preemption are unspecified.
baselines: existing GPU WCET analyses assuming deterministic warp paths
relaxed scheduling bounds without the practical warp constraint
limits: The description omits schedulability impact, exactness proof scope, kernel/memory coverage, and hardware validation.
Tighter bounds rely on a practical warp-execution constraint whose deployability and enforcement cost are unspecified.
Official description only; real-time guarantees require paper-level proof and platform verification.

title: Compiler Framework for Directional Transport in Zoned Neutral-Atom Systems with AOD Assistance: A Hybrid Remote CZ Approach
evidence_span: The compiler reserves AOD shuttling for channel setup and micro-tuning while using detuning-modulated directional transport of a Rydberg excitation through a resettable ancilla corridor for remote CZ gates; the description claims approximately 50–90% shorter entangling stages than AOD-only baselines and long-distance connectivity.
problem: AOD-based neutral-atom shuttling is constrained by non-crossing paths, device speed, and field-of-view/NA limits, restricting long-distance entanglement.
method_or_artifact: Hybrid compiler and gate scheme combining AOD assistance with directional Rydberg-excitation transport through dynamic ancilla corridors.
workload_or_benchmark: Zoned neutral-atom arrays executing remote CZ gates; atom counts, layouts, fidelity/error rates, transport schedules, and compiler baselines are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Rydberg neutral-atom system with AODs, antiblockade, detuning-modulated pi pulses, and resettable ancillas; optical hardware, coherence, and calibration assumptions are unspecified.
metrics: Long-distance connectivity beyond objective-limited shuttling claimed qualitatively
limits: The description omits gate fidelity, atom-loss/error impact, corridor overhead, distance scaling, and compilation/runtime costs.
Duration reduction may trade against calibration complexity, ancilla use, or error accumulation.
Official description only; quantum-control claims require experimental or detailed simulation verification.

title: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Real-Time BEV-Based 3D Object Detection
evidence_span: The hardware-constrained NAS framework combines a lightweight depth estimator and LiDAR-camera cross-attention for BEV fusion; on nuScenes it reports 70.1% mAP, a 2.3-point improvement over baseline, and 35.6 FPS on Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin.
problem: High-accuracy BEV 3D detection models often run below real-time rates on practical edge platforms.
method_or_artifact: Hardware-aware neural architecture search with a lightweight depth network and LiDAR-camera cross-attention in BEV conversion.
workload_or_benchmark: nuScenes multimodal LiDAR/camera 3D object detection on Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin; model suite, input resolution, power mode, and baseline configuration are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: Resource-limited edge inference on Jetson AGX Orin with LiDAR-camera fusion; software stack, memory use, power, and thermal conditions are unspecified.
metrics: 35.6 FPS on Nvidia Jetson AGX Orin
limits: The description omits latency distribution, energy, accuracy breakdown, search cost, and baseline model/hardware settings.
Real-time suitability depends on sensor rate, input resolution, power mode, and end-to-end preprocessing/postprocessing.
Official description only; deployment claims require reproducible benchmark conditions.

title: CHiRM-DSE: CodeLLM-Based Hierarchical and Rule-Mining Guided DSE for FPGA Accelerators
evidence_span: CHiRM-DSE mines rules to guide HLS pragma exploration, decomposes the design space to prune candidates, and uses a CodeLLM evaluator that is faster than direct HLS and more accurate than prior GNN evaluators; four HLS benchmarks show better QoR than state of the art under equal time budgets, with demo code released publicly.
problem: HLS pragma spaces are large and expensive to evaluate, while exhaustive, hyperparameter-sensitive, or poorly portable search strategies limit FPGA accelerator DSE.
method_or_artifact: Hierarchical design-space decomposition, rule-mining-guided search, and CodeLLM-based design-point evaluation for HLS accelerator DSE.
workload_or_benchmark: Four widely used HLS benchmarks and FPGA accelerator pragma spaces; benchmark names, time budgets, QoR metrics, HLS tools, and state-of-the-art baselines are unspecified.
hardware_or_process_assumptions: HLS-to-FPGA accelerator flow with synthesis directives and QoR evaluation; FPGA family, tool version, synthesis settings, and implementation conditions are unspecified.
metrics: Better QoR under the same time budget claimed qualitatively
CodeLLM evaluator faster than direct HLS and more accurate than prior GNN evaluator claimed qualitatively
limits: The description omits numeric QoR, search-time, evaluator-accuracy, hardware, and reproducibility details.
CodeLLM surrogate quality may depend on benchmark similarity, prompt/training leakage, and tool/version conventions.
Official description only; DSE superiority and artifact claims require paper-level and artifact verification.
